title: Queen against rook II: how to reach Philidor
summary: The ladder that walks the king to the edge, the second-rank defence and the diagonal position.
part.second.title: The second-rank defence
part.second.summary: The rook cuts off our king. The first moves, and the stalemate waiting for whoever squeezes too hard.
part.defenses.title: The king's defences
part.defenses.summary: Whichever way the black king goes: check to gain time, king one step forward, until Philidor.
part.diagonal.title: The diagonal and the rook's checks
part.diagonal.summary: A queen triangle leads to Philidor, and a quiet move takes away the rook's checks.
part.ladder.title: The ladder
part.ladder.summary: Far from the edge: check, check, and the king steps down. Then the whole ending in the practical challenge.
step.t_second: The rook, on the rank next to the black king, cuts off our king. Think: how do you bring our king forward without running into a string of checks or stalemating the black king?
step.t_second.hint1: A queen check first, to shift the black king; then a quiet king move, sideways.
step.intro: Last lesson you won from the Philidor position. Today is the road to it. This is the second-rank defence: the black king is on the edge and the rook, on the rank next to it, cuts off our king. As long as it stays there our king cannot get in, and the rook also threatens checks on b7 and e6. Euwe published this position in 1958. It is a win, and there is one aim: bring our king in front of the black king and reach Philidor.
step.stale: First, what not to do. Here the queen went to d6, too close. The rook checked on b7, the king went to c6 and the rook offered itself on b6. If the king takes, the black king is stalemated. If the queen takes, the same. And if the king runs, the checks never end. A draw. The rule from last lesson still holds: queen far, king near.
step.open: The first two moves are learned by heart. A queen check along the diagonal, which sends the king to d8, and then a quiet king move, sideways and not forward.
step.open.hint: 1.Qf5+ and, after 1...Kd8, 2.Kc5. On c6 the king would be checked by the rook from e6.
step.open.done: Look at the king on c5: the rook has no good check, and the black king has to choose a side.
step.fork3: From here Black has three defences. The king returns to c7. Or the king runs the other way, via e8. Or the rook leaves the king and goes far away to check from behind. Let us see the first two move by move. In both the pattern is the same: the queen checks to gain time, the king steps forward, and Philidor appears at the end.
step.a1: The black king returned to c7. Centralise the queen on d5. After the rook comes to d7, check on e5 and walk the king to b5.
step.a1.hint: 1.Qd5, then 2.Qe5+ and 3.Kb5. The white king goes round along the b-file.
step.a1.done: The black king is already on the b-file, and our king is beside it. Now the queen has to be brought into place.
step.a2: Now the move that is hard to find: the queen goes to e8, behind everything, and takes squares from the black king. Then it returns to e4, the king enters on c6 and the queen closes in on d5 and d8.
step.a2.hint: 1.Qe8, 2.Qe4, 3.Kc6, 4.Qd5 and 5.Qd8. At the end the black king is on a7 with the rook on b7, and our king on c6.
step.a2.done: Look at the position sideways: black king and rook on the edge, our king a knight's move away, queen on the file beside them. It is Philidor, on the a-file, with Black to move. The rook falls.
step.c1: Second defence: the black king runs via e8. Chase it with a check on c8 and bring the king to d6. When the rook goes to a7, a new check on c4 and the king advances to e6.
step.c1.hint: 1.Qc8+, 2.Kd6, 3.Qc4+ and 4.Ke6. A check to gain time, the king one step forward.
step.c1.done: The black king has been pushed to the other corner, and our king went with it, always in front.
step.c2: Finish it. Check on c5, queen to the centre on d5, and the king enters on f6 uncovering the queen's check. Then the triangle you already know: h1 and h5.
step.c2.done: Philidor again, now in the g8 corner. Two different defences, the same ending.
step.checks: The third defence is for the rook to run far away and give checks. The answer is a principle that holds for the whole endgame: before advancing the king, take the checking squares away from the rook. In this position from Nunn the black king and rook are on the second rank and our king wants f6, but the rook would check on g7 and g6 without end.
step.quiet: Instead of checking, prepare. The queen goes to d8 and then to d4, from where it watches g7. Only then does the king go in, and the rook's checks are over in two moves.
step.quiet.hint: 1.Qd8 and, after 1...Kh7, 2.Qd4. To the rook checks the king answers f6 and f7.
step.quiet.done: The checks are over, and the rook is stuck next to its king. A quiet queen move is worth more than a check: Smerdon says the moves that make most progress in this endgame are hardly ever checks.
step.t_diagonal: Black king, rook, our king and queen, all four on the same diagonal. The queen threatens a discovered check. Think: what is missing for it to work, and how do you get it?
step.t_diagonal.hint1: The position is good, but the move is not. You have seen the queen lose a tempo with a triangle.
step.diagonal: One more position to remember: the diagonal. Black king, rook, our king and queen, all four on the same diagonal. The queen is ready to give a discovered check as soon as our king steps aside. But it is our move, and we need it to be Black's. You know the cure: a queen triangle.
step.discover: Pass the move with the queen: f4, check on f5 and back to e5. The rook will have to go to b7; then the king goes to c6 with discovered check, and the queen closes in on a1 and a5.
step.discover.done: Philidor, with Black to move. The diagonal position is six moves away from it.
step.t_ladder: The black king is still far from the edge, on the rook's file. Think: how do you push it rank by rank, without giving the rook room for checks?
step.t_ladder.hint1: Think in three beats: two by the queen, with check, and one by our king.
step.ladder: And when the black king is still far from the edge? This is where the ladder comes in. This position is from Walter Browne's rematch against the computer Belle, in 1978. The black king and rook are on the same file; our king is on the same rank as the black king, two files away. The recipe has three beats: check, check, and the king steps down one square. The position repeats one rank closer to the edge.
step.climb: Go down the ladder twice. Check on g7, check on h6, king to e4. And again: check on g6, check on h5, king to e3.
step.climb.hint: 1.Qg7+, 2.Qh6+, 3.Ke4. Then 4.Qg6+, 5.Qh5+, 6.Ke3. The queen checks from behind; the king only moves once the black king is back on the rook's file.
step.climb.done: The black king left the fifth rank and reached the third without being able to do anything. One more rung and it reaches the second rank, next to the edge, where the rook runs out of room: that is how Browne won the bet, on the last move allowed.
step.recap: Three ideas to take away. One: against the second rank, check on f5 and king sideways; then a check to gain time and the king one step forward, until Philidor. Two: before advancing the king, take the rook's checks away with a quiet queen move. Three: far from the edge, the ladder: check, check, king steps down. And the queen never hugs the cornered king.
step.finish: Your turn in the practical challenge, from the second-rank defence. Start with the two moves you know by heart and see which defence it picks. If it lets the rook loose, take the checks away before advancing.
ex.e12: White to move. A position from Nunn: the rook left the black king and has just checked on d1. Bring our king to the sixth rank without taking more checks.
ex.e12.hint: Before the king moves, a quiet queen move to the centre, from where she watches the b-file along both diagonals.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Qe4 and, after 1...Rd7, 2.Kc6. From e4 the queen takes b7 and b1, and the rook loses the checks that mattered; the king enters on c6 attacking the rook, which goes back to b7. From there, 3.Qe8+ and 4.Qd8: Philidor. It is the same quiet move as in the lesson, in a position the lesson did not show.
ex.e05: White to move. The black king is near the corner with the rook beside it. Find a queen move that gives the rook no check.
ex.e05.hint: The most natural check leaves the black king in the corner and our king with a single entry square. Look at what the rook does on that square.
ex.e05.solution: 1.Qe5 (or 1.Qd4). The queen stays far away and controls the central squares; the rook has no useful check. After 1.Qc6+ and 2.Kb6 the rook checks on a6 and any capture is stalemate: Berger's trap, from 1889.
ex.e13: White to move. Second-rank defence, but instead of guarding its king the rook ran away to e1, and three queen checks have already driven the black king to c8. Find the move that stops the rook from rejoining its king.
ex.e13.hint: Look at how the rook would come back: along the c-file or through the squares near its king. One queen square cuts off both.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Qc4! It is not a check: the queen takes the c-file and the diagonal to e2, and the rook cannot rejoin its king. From here the checks end in a fork: 1...Kc7 2.Qf4+ Kc8 3.Qg4+ Kd8 4.Qh4+, and the rook on e1 falls. More checks instead of 1.Qc4 only let the rook come back. The line is Euwe's, as Wikipedia gives it.
ex.e14: White to move. The rook's other escape: after 1.Qf5+ Kd8 2.Kc5, Black played 2...Re1 and the queen checked on d3. The rook will still give checks. Walk the king up to the black king without losing time.
ex.e14.hint: Our king climbs the d-file. The queen checks only to gain time, and one quiet queen move takes squares from the black king; when the rook checks, step towards the black king, not away from it.
ex.e14.solution: 4.Kd5, 5.Qf3+, 6.Qg4 (a quiet move), 7.Qf4+ and 8.Kd6; against the checks, 9.Ke6 and 10.Kf6. With our king right next to the black king, the rook runs out of checks and falls to a fork: 10...Re2 11.Qa4+ and 12.Qd1+. It is Euwe's defence B, as Wikipedia gives it.
ex.e15: White to move. Hannes Stefánsson against Karsten Müller, 1992: the black king is in the centre and the rook cuts our king off. In the game White played 74.Qe7 and lost four moves. Find the shortest way to the second-rank defence.
ex.e15.hint: A queen check along the fifth rank first; then our king walks, and the queen checks again only when the black king can be pushed to the seventh.
ex.e15.solution: 74.Qb5+, 75.Kg5, 76.Kf5, 77.Qb6+ and 78.Kf6. The check sends the black king back, our king climbs the f-file while the rook stays on the e-file, and the last check pushes the black king to the seventh rank. After 78...Kc8 79.Qa6+ Rb7 80.Ke6, it is the second rank from the lesson. The improvement is Nunn's, quoted by Wikipedia.
ex.e16: White to move. A position from Nunn: the black king went to the edge and the rook is far from it, on the h-file. Find the move that makes three threats at once.
ex.e16.hint: It is not a check. Look for a square from which the queen threatens mate and attacks the rook, and notice that the rook has no good check.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Qf8! It threatens 2.Qa8 mate and 2.Qxh6, and the rook's squares turn bad: almost every rook move allows the mate on a8. The most stubborn defence is 1...Rh5+; then the king goes to c6, and no further, to stop the checks. After 2...Ka7, 3.Qf7+ and the rook falls. Nunn calls it a "triple threat"; it is in ColinParker's study on Lichess.
key.second: The black rook defends beside its king, on the second rank, and looks solid. With a well-chosen queen check and the white king coming closer, White takes this defence apart.
key.diagonal: The rook is glued to the black king, on the diagonal. The queen makes a little triangle to pass the move and reaches the Philidor position, the classic winning set-up.
key.ladder: The ladder: two queen checks and one king step, then again, until the black king reaches the edge of the board. That is how Browne beat Belle in 1978.
history: Queen against rook looks easy, since the queen is worth so much more. In practice it is one of the hardest endings to win: the rook, glued to its king, can hold out for a long time and gives checks from every direction. It was a computer that showed the world how hard it is. In December 1978 Ken Thompson's Belle defended the rook against grandmaster Walter Browne, who failed to win within the fifty-move limit. In the rematch, at the end of that same month, Browne drove the black king to the edge with a ladder of checks and captured the rook on exactly the fiftieth move. Decades earlier, former world champion Max Euwe had already studied the rook's defences.
practice: The second-rank defence, against the clock or without it. You know the first two moves by heart; from there, a check to gain time, the king one step forward, and Philidor.
